welcome.title: Energy Accounting
welcome.description: We help you find your personal energy budget. Through a few short questions we assess your current level of function and create a tailored starting point.
welcome.feature_bell_sub: Based on the Bell Disability Scale (Bell, 1995)
welcome.feature_day_sub: Based on DePaul Energy Envelope theory (Jason et al.)
welcome.feature_anchors_sub: Concrete examples of what each point represents
welcome.duration_note: Takes about 3–5 minutes. You can adjust your budget at any time.

bell.title: Your level of function
bell.description: Choose the description that best fits your current situation in a typical week. Based on Dr David Bell's function scale, a validated tool used in ME/CFS research since 1995.
bell.note: Adapted from Dr David Bell's CFIDS Disability Scale, used in research and clinical practice worldwide.
bell.level_80_desc: Mild symptoms on exertion. Can work full-time but notices activities cost more than before. Normal daily life with some limitations during demanding activities.
bell.level_60_desc: Mild to moderate symptoms at rest. Clear daily limitations. Can work full-time with light duties if schedule is flexible, or part-time with heavier work.
bell.level_40_desc: Moderate symptoms at rest, worse with activity. Manages 3–4 hours of light activity per day with breaks. Not housebound, but needs a lot of rest.
bell.level_20_desc: Moderate to severe symptoms at rest. Housebound most of the time. Manages 1–2 hours of light activity per day. Difficulty concentrating.
bell.level_10_desc: Severe symptoms at rest. Bedridden most of the day. Very limited capacity for activity and concentration.

typical_day.title: How do you manage everyday activities?
typical_day.description: Think about a typical day over the past week. How much do these activities cost you? This mapping is inspired by the DePaul group's energy envelope research.
typical_day.info: You don't need to answer all of them — answer the ones relevant to you. The important thing is to give an honest picture of how you experience it, not how you 'should' manage.
typical_day.work_desc: Work, study, admin, or demanding conversations
typical_day.ability_manageable: Manage it, but feel it afterwards
typical_day.ability_difficult: Demanding, need a long rest after
typical_day.ability_impossible: Can't manage this at the moment

energy_anchors.title: What do the points mean?
energy_anchors.description: For your energy budget to be useful, you need concrete reference points. Here are suggestions for what each point level represents. You can calibrate these to your own experience.
energy_anchors.info: These examples are a starting point. The energy cost of an activity varies from person to person. Over time you will calibrate your own values based on experience.
energy_anchors.anchor_1_ex4: Lying down reading a few pages

budget_result.title: Your energy budget
budget_result.description: Based on your answers we have calculated a suggested daily energy budget. You can adjust it up or down.
budget_result.advice: Remember: This is a starting point, not a fixed answer. Research recommends starting conservatively and adjusting over 1–2 weeks based on whether you experience PEM/crashes. The goal is to find a level where you can be consistently active without overloading.
budget_result.example_header: With {{budget}} points a day might look like

confirm.title: All set!
confirm.description: Your daily budget is set to {{budget}} points.
confirm.tip1_text: Spend the first week logging without changing routines. It gives valuable data about your actual usage pattern.
confirm.tip2_text: Experiencing regular crashes/PEM? Reduce the budget. Have surplus energy? You can carefully increase it.
confirm.tip3_text: Rest, nature and meditation add energy back. Plan these in as part of your day.
